objectives.text: Describe how the light-dependent reactions convert light energy into ATP and NADPH.

quiz.title: Week 3 Quiz: The Light Reactions
quiz.instructions: Four questions on the light-dependent reactions. Every question links back to this week's reading.

entry.title: Products of the light reactions
entry.item_body: Which pair of molecules is produced by the light-dependent reactions and then used by the Calvin cycle?

feedback.correct: Right. The light reactions bank energy as ATP and reducing power as NADPH; the Calvin cycle spends both to fix carbon.
feedback.incorrect: Re-read the handoff between the two stages. The light reactions make the fuel; the Calvin cycle makes the sugar.

answer_feedback.3f1b8c22-9f1a-4d3e-8b5a-1c2d3e4f5a6b: Correct — these are the two energy carriers passed to the Calvin cycle.
answer_feedback.7c4e2a91-0b6d-4f8c-a2e1-9d8c7b6a5f4e: NADH is respiration's carrier. Photosynthesis uses NADPH — one phosphate different, different pathway.
answer_feedback.b2d9f6e3-5a7c-4e1b-9f3d-2c8a1b0e7d4f: These are outputs of photosynthesis overall, not of the light reactions specifically. Glucose comes later, in the Calvin cycle.

entry.title: Source of released oxygen
entry.item_body: The oxygen released during photosynthesis comes from splitting carbon dioxide.

feedback.correct: Correct. The oxygen comes from splitting water at Photosystem II, replacing electrons chlorophyll lost to light.
feedback.incorrect: A common mix-up. Carbon dioxide is split in the Calvin cycle, but the oxygen you breathe comes from water.

entry.title: Events at the thylakoid membrane
entry.item_body: Select every event that happens at the thylakoid membrane during the light-dependent reactions.

choices.item_body: Protons are pumped into the thylakoid space
Water is split to replace lost electrons
Carbon dioxide is fixed into a three-carbon sugar

feedback.correct: Both correct events happen in the membrane. The other two belong to the Calvin cycle, out in the stroma.
feedback.incorrect: Sort each event by location: light reactions happen in the thylakoid membrane, the Calvin cycle happens in the stroma.

entry.title: Predicting the effect of blocking ATP synthase
entry.item_body: A researcher adds a chemical that punctures the thylakoid membrane, letting protons leak freely across it. Explain what happens to ATP production in the light reactions, and why.

scoring_data.value: Full credit: student states ATP production falls or stops, AND explains that ATP synthase depends on the proton gradient — leaking protons collapse the gradient, so there is no stored energy to drive the enzyme. Half credit: correct outcome, no mechanism.

feedback.neutral: The key move is connecting the proton gradient to ATP synthase: no gradient, no ATP. This is the same mechanism you saw in cellular respiration.
